title: Revising the Shuttle Notice
text:
A college transportation office is rewriting a notice about changes to its evening shuttle. The first draft was assembled from several emails, so it repeats information and uses transitions that do not always match the relationship between sentences. The editor wants students to understand the change quickly because many will read the notice on a phone while walking between buildings.

The revised notice should state the new departure time once, explain why the schedule changed, and tell riders where to find live updates. Repeating “at this point in time,” “due to the fact that,” and similar phrases makes the message longer without making it clearer. The editor replaces these expressions with shorter wording when no meaning is lost.

Transitions require a different kind of decision. “However” should introduce a contrast, while “therefore” should introduce a result. “For example” should lead into an illustration of the previous idea. A transition that sounds formal but names the wrong relationship can mislead a reader even if the grammar around it is correct. The final version should be concise, but it should never remove a condition, exception, or logical connection that riders need in order to act correctly.
